title: Durable OS-protected recovery key provider surviving process restart
description:
Objective: supply the durable, OS-protected key/identity provider that the recovery chain has been missing, so a PREPARED restore command can resume after process death with the SAME key epoch. Authored by governor-36019faa on human direction 2026-08-10, from architect-5b5302ee's audit (comment-1a16d3a86ddb40e29b6a62d83e33897a) and architect-8ee37119's re-verification (comment-9f416aa2f693470ea2de4f6a9635d979), both on task-b6e3dd2af916490fb2bc4d375a530683.

THE PRODUCTION SOURCE NAMES THIS TASK ITSELF. apps/daemon/src/recovery/recovery-incarnation.ts, in its own header comment above createRecoveryIncarnationService (:63), states: "MINTED carries authority: NONE and is process-local. It is a proposal for RecoveryAnchor to persist; nothing here is durable, and a non-extractable WebCrypto key behind a handle is protected against export but is NOT an OS-durable keystore reference - it does not survive the process. A later controller must supply a protected durable key provider before anything can claim crash-resume." This task is that provider. Do not treat the quoted sentence as a design suggestion; it is the acceptance boundary.

MEASURED AT HEAD bec1cc6 by governor-36019faa, re-verify before planning (the staleness rail binds in both directions):
- createRecoveryIncarnationService keeps `settled` and `inFlight` as in-process `new Map` (recovery-incarnation.ts:66-67). Restart loses both.
- The key handle resolves to key material through a module-private WeakMap in recovery-incarnation.node.ts; only the PUBLIC key is exported via webcrypto.subtle.exportKey("spki", publicKey).
- recovery-incarnation.test.ts POSITIVELY ASSERTS that the signing handle stays out of the serialized binding. DO NOT PLAN TO PERSIST KEY MATERIAL - a landed test forbids it and any such plan goes red.
- apps/daemon/src/recovery/ already contains recovery-succession.ts and recovery-incarnation-anchor.ts. Read both before naming any new file; task-304aa634 landed succession proof and this task must compose it rather than mint a parallel mechanism.

THE HARD PART, stated so it is not planned around: Node provides no portable Windows/macOS/Linux ACL or keystore primitive. POSIX mode bits plus a final-file fsync do NOT prove OS protection on win32. A plan that claims OS protection without a platform-specific mechanism, or that silently degrades to a plain file, is the "proof that only proves the shapes" that epic Clause 2 forbids. If a supported host cannot provide the guarantee, the correct outcome is a typed UNKNOWN that refuses with a stable code - never an optimistic pass.

NOT IN SCOPE: the two-slot anchor installer itself (task-b6e3dd2a), store schema rows, the daemon restore controller, generating backup bytes, external-effect inventory, R3 completion.

Hard dependencies: none. This is the root of the chain and is plannable now.

Owned paths: apps/daemon/src/recovery/ - a new focused provider module plus its .js bridge and focused tests. Do not edit recovery-incarnation.ts's existing exports beyond what composition requires.

Verification: pnpm --filter @moe/daemon typecheck && pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test
definitionOfDone: A durable key/identity provider persists a key epoch and reopens the SAME epoch after full process death on every supported host (win32, darwin, linux), demonstrated by a test that actually terminates and restarts a process rather than simulating it.

Protection is OS-backed and platform-specific, not POSIX mode bits on win32; the mechanism used per platform is named in code and asserted. A host that cannot provide the guarantee yields a typed UNKNOWN refusing with a distinct stable code and layer, never an optimistic pass.

Private key material is never serialized into any binding or anchor payload; the existing recovery-incarnation.test.ts assertion that the signing handle stays out of the serialized binding still passes unchanged.
The provider composes the landed succession surface (apps/daemon/src/recovery/recovery-succession.ts) rather than minting a second incarnation mechanism; the composition point is named and tested.
Every refusal path asserts its exact stable reason code AND the refusing layer, and each declared failure injection is generated at least once (a sweep producing zero cases must fail).
Mutating each production guard turns a NAMED focused test red; the drill is run, reverted, and the exact failing assertion text recorded.
Fresh pnpm --filter @moe/daemon typecheck && pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test exits 0.
taskRails: Authoritative design is D:/projexts/moes/docs/plans/2026-08-05-moe-rebuild-design.md SHA-256 1D9D1EC97D3F07247FBBC088045E0BA2FD6DA8307F10A9026C55106419383191; do not edit it.
Do not persist private key material anywhere. Succession (re-mint and prove the chain from the predecessor) is the sanctioned answer to process death, not resurrection of a prior key.
Do not claim POSIX directory-fsync or ACL semantics on win32. Name the actual per-platform mechanism.

Cross-package symbol use must prove the DEPENDENCY EDGE, not just the symbol: manifest declaration, lockfile importer entry, and a compiled bare-specifier probe deleted in the same command. Three tasks died on this board today for skipping it.
Target <=250 physical lines per production source and split before 400; this cap is per file, never per task.

READ-ONLY. Composition surfaces re-measured at HEAD; all five architect line refs hold.

SUCCESSION (recovery-succession.ts): verifyAnchoredPredecessor :53, mintSuccessor :107, proveSuccession :131, readSuccessionChain :233, createRecoverySuccessionService :322. Confirmed the four-step order inside `succeed` (:332-356) is verify -> mint -> anchorIncarnation -> proveSuccession -> commitSuccession.

DECISION forced by the plan's own drills: compose the FOUR EXPORTED FUNCTIONS individually rather than calling `createRecoverySuccessionService(...).succeed`. Reason — `succeed` destroys the successor handle in a `finally` (:363-365) and returns no handle, and more decisively drills (b)/(c)/(d) require verifyAnchoredPredecessor / mintSuccessor / proveSuccession to be MY call sites: if the provider delegated to `succeed`, mutating my file could not redden those cases and the only way to run the drill would be editing a landed foreign file in a shared worktree. `commitSuccession` is module-private, so the provider commits the record itself using ONLY exported contract symbols (RECOVERY_SUCCESSION_COMMAND_KIND, successionAggregateId, RECOVERY_SUCCESSION_SCHEMA_VERSION) and the SAME `recovery-succeed:<pred>:<succ>` command-id format — the aggregate is keyed on the PREDECESSOR with expectedVersion 0, so the STORE still refuses a fork across both writers. The write is then verified by read-back through the LANDED `readSuccessionChain`, so the production surface proving the chain is theirs, not mine.

VOCABULARY: reuse SUCCESSION_PREDECESSOR_NOT_FOUND / _UNVERIFIABLE / _PROOF_UNAVAILABLE / _ANCHOR_UNAVAILABLE / _ALREADY_RECORDED verbatim (they keep layer RECOVERY_SUCCESSION, and my tests assert that layer). Mint only what succession does not model: RECOVERY_KEY_EPOCH_INPUT_INVALID (succession's input refusal literally says "must name exactly one predecessor incarnation" — my request must NOT name one, so reusing it would be false evidence), RECOVERY_KEY_PROTECTION_UNAVAILABLE, RECOVERY_KEY_PROTECTION_UNVERIFIABLE, RECOVERY_KEY_EPOCH_POINTER_UNREADABLE.

DURABILITY: readAnchoredIncarnation :147 / anchorIncarnation :186, both through SqliteEventStore. No second substrate. HEAD DISCOVERY is the one genuinely missing durable fact — a process that died holds nothing, and every incarnationRef is entropy-derived so none can be recomputed. Solved with ONE new aggregate on the SAME substrate: `recovery-key-epoch:<digestOf("key-epoch-pointer", projectId, restoreCommandId)>`, deterministically addressable from the restore command alone, read via `store.readEvents(aggregateId)` (no full scan) and advanced with expectedVersion = generation so a lost race refuses rather than forks. Store API verified: SqliteEventStore.openForProject(path, projectId) (recovery-succession.test.ts:55), readEvents(aggregateId): readonly StoredEvent[] (sqlite-event-store.ts:308), StoredEvent.payload: Uint8Array (store-contracts.ts:170), getAggregateVersion (:266).

PLATFORM MECHANISM probed live on this win32 host before committing to it: `icacls <dir> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<domain\user>:(OI)(CI)F"` then `icacls <dir>` read-back returns exactly one ACE, `YARON-PC\Yaron:(OI)(CI)(F)`, with NO `(I)` inherited marker (before: four ACEs, all `(I)`). That is a real Win32 DACL, not POSIX mode bits. POSIX hosts get chmod 0o700 + stat read-back on mode AND uid. Anything else -> typed UNKNOWN.

CONVENTION: `.node.ts` sibling for host code (recovery-incarnation / .node, doctor-version / .node); every non-test module has a one-line LF `.js` bridge (12 present, 12 modules).

recovery-key-provider-contract.ts — types and frozen vocabulary only; no host calls, no crypto, no store I/O.
- RECOVERY_KEY_PROVIDER_LAYER = "RECOVERY_KEY_PROVIDER" (the refusing-layer half of DoD 5).
- RECOVERY_KEY_PROVIDER_ERROR_CODES frozen tuple of exactly four minted codes; the header states why each of the four is not modelled by succession and why every other fault propagates a succession refusal verbatim WITH ITS OWN LAYER.
- RECOVERY_KEY_PROTECTION_MECHANISMS is a CLOSED union — "WIN32_DACL_EXPLICIT_OWNER_ONLY" | "POSIX_MODE_0700_OWNER_ONLY" — plus a separate RecoveryKeyProtectionUnknown member carrying mechanism:"UNKNOWN", truth:"UNKNOWN", a fixed code and this layer. Never a boolean: the comment records that a boolean lets a host that applied nothing report the same `true` as one that applied a real DACL.
- RecoveryKeyProviderPort = { protect(directoryPath): Promise<RecoveryKeyProtectionResult> } — the single host boundary the `.node.ts` implements.
- Refusal factories are fixed-text, so a caught `icacls` message or a path has no route into evidence; the ONLY observed value admitted is the platform, narrowed by asHostPlatform to win32|darwin|linux|OTHER first.
- RecoveryKeyEpochRequest carries NO predecessorIncarnationRef and no keyHandle by construction, and snapshotKeyEpochRequest refuses extra keys — mirroring snapshotSuccessionRequest's descriptor-based single read.

recovery-key-epoch-store.ts — the durable I/O, all on the SAME SqliteEventStore substrate (no second substrate).
- keyEpochAggregateId(projectId, restoreCommandId) = "recovery-key-epoch:" + digestOf("key-epoch-pointer", projectId, restoreCommandId). Digested, not concatenated, because restoreCommandId is caller-chosen and a raw suffix would let a caller steer the aggregate id.
- readKeyEpochPointer returns THREE distinct states, ABSENT | PRESENT | UNREADABLE, as separate union members. Collapsing UNREADABLE into ABSENT is what would silently mint a second epoch for one restore command; `mem:gotcha-empty-absent-unreadable-need-three-answers` is the reason this is a union rather than `pointer | null`, and step 4 will pin distinctness with a Set-size assertion rather than three independent arms.
- writeKeyEpochPointer advances with expectedVersion = pointer.generation, so two processes racing to reopen one epoch both read N and the STORE lets exactly one write N+1. No try/catch, matching anchorIncarnation.
- commitSuccessionRecord reproduces recovery-succession.ts's module-private writer on its own terms EXACTLY: same command kind, same predecessor-keyed aggregate via the exported successionAggregateId, same expectedVersion 0, same `recovery-succeed:<pred>:<succ>` command id. Matching the terms is what keeps the store's fork refusal effective across both writers.

createRecoveryKeyProvider(crypto, port) — both dependencies INJECTED, zero host-specific code, no import of any node: module. `open(store, request)` in order:
1. snapshotKeyEpochRequest -> KEY_EPOCH_INPUT_INVALID. Extra keys refused, not trimmed.
2. port.protect -> a fault NEVER becomes a success. A throwing port maps to protectionUnavailable(port.platform) rather than to OTHER, which is why the port declares `platform` separately.
3. readKeyEpochPointer -> UNREADABLE refuses; ABSENT is the cold start; PRESENT is the reopen.
4. Reopen composes the four landed exports IN THE PLANNED ORDER and reimplements none of them: verifyAnchoredPredecessor -> mintSuccessor -> anchorIncarnation -> proveSuccession, then commitSuccessionRecord, then the pointer advance.
5. finish() reads readSuccessionChain — THE LANDED READER IS THE AUTHORITY ON THE ORIGIN, not my pointer. If the chain's origin disagrees with the pointer's, the pointer has drifted and the open is REFUSED rather than believed; believing it would rename the epoch identity everything downstream fences against. chainLength also comes from that reader.

Fail-closed audit of every path: input invalid, protection unavailable/unverifiable/throwing, pointer unreadable, pointer cycle, unanchored head, unverifiable predecessor, unmintable successor, anchor refused, proof refused, succession conflict, pointer-advance conflict — each returns a code AND a layer and writes nothing. The successor handle is destroyed on every non-success path (`keep` flag plus explicit discards after the pointer advance and after finish), and kept alive only when an epoch is actually returned.

Two additions beyond the literal step text, both forced by correctness rather than preference:
- resolveHead() + readRecordedSuccessor(). ANCHOR -> RECORD -> ADVANCE is three writes; a death between the second and third leaves a head that has ALREADY been succeeded, and the retry would lose to expectedVersion 0 forever and wedge the epoch permanently. Following the succession records forward heals it. This makes the pointer a hint and the succession records the authority, which is the right direction for DoD 4. A revisited ref is treated as a damaged log (refusal), not a newer head. Covered by the "crash between the succession record and the pointer advance heals" case.
- The provider does NOT re-export its .node port yet; that lands in step 6 with the module, following recovery-incarnation.ts's precedent.

One test fix during GREEN, and it was a real vacuity bug in my own assertion, not a production change: the forbidden-token list used "d\":" to catch a JWK private scalar, but that substring also matches the tail of `backupGenerationDigest":` — so it failed against perfectly clean bytes. Corrected to the quoted form '"d":' with a comment. Also moved each injection's setup into an `arrange` hook that runs BEFORE the decision-count snapshot, so seeding a fixture is not miscounted as a write by the "nothing was written on a refusal" assertion.

implementationPlan.description:
The platform port: apps/daemon/src/recovery/recovery-key-provider.node.ts plus its LF `.js` bridge. This is where DoD 2 is won or lost.

STATE THE HONEST CONSTRAINT IN CODE, as recovery-incarnation.node.ts does: Node exposes NO portable Windows/macOS/Linux ACL or keystore primitive. Therefore implement DETECTION plus a NAMED mechanism per platform, and a typed UNKNOWN everywhere else:
  - win32: POSIX mode bits are meaningless here. If you cannot name and verify a real Win32 mechanism, the honest result is the typed UNKNOWN refusal — the task text blesses this explicitly and forbids the alternative. Do NOT claim protection you cannot demonstrate, and do NOT claim directory-fsync semantics (taskRail 3).

{"platform":"win32","result":{"mechanism":"WIN32_DACL_EXPLICIT_OWNER_ONLY","ok":true,"platform":"win32"}}
So the win32 branch is a demonstrated mechanism, not a claim. Step 7 pins it as an assertion.

WIN32 — a REAL Win32 discretionary ACL, named WIN32_DACL_EXPLICIT_OWNER_ONLY, not POSIX mode bits (taskRail 3):
- `icacls <dir> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<whoami>:(OI)(CI)F"`. `/inheritance:r` removes every inherited ACE; `/grant:r` replaces grants, leaving one explicit ACE for the account this process runs as.
- The identity comes from System32\whoami.exe, NOT %USERNAME%/%USERDOMAIN% — an environment variable is caller-owned and this decides who keeps access. Both tools are resolved under %SystemRoot%\System32 rather than PATH, and a missing tool is UNAVAILABLE.
- THE READ-BACK IS THE ASSERTION, because icacls exiting 0 only proves the tool ran. A volume without ACL support (FAT32, exFAT, some redirectors) accepts the call and keeps its inherited ACL. Protection is claimed ONLY when the re-read shows exactly ONE ACE, principal case-insensitively equal to the whoami identity, carrying (F) and NOT carrying (I). Measured before/after on a real temp dir while planning: before = 4 ACEs all flagged (I); after = one ACE `YARON-PC\Yaron:(OI)(CI)(F)` with no (I).
- The parser reads only the ACL block and stops at the blank line, so the localized "Successfully processed" summary is never parsed; an unrecognised dialect returns null and becomes UNVERIFIABLE rather than protected.

DARWIN/LINUX — POSIX_MODE_0700_OWNER_ONLY: chmod 0o700 then stat read-back requiring (mode & 0o777) === 0o700 AND uid === process.getuid(). chmod succeeding proves the syscall was accepted, not that the filesystem honours mode bits (FAT/exFAT/9p/SMB report a fixed mode), which is why the stat decides. An absent getuid is an unverified owner, never an assumed one.

ANY OTHER PLATFORM — no detection, no fallback, no mode bits pretending to be an ACL: typed UNKNOWN via protectionUnavailable(platform).

Header states the honest constraint the way recovery-incarnation.node.ts states its own — Node exposes no portable ACL or keystore primitive, so there is nothing to call that means the same thing on three platforms — and states what is actually protected: no private key material is persisted anywhere, the durable record holds PUBLIC bytes, so the property is ACCESS RESTRICTION against other local users while tamper-EVIDENCE comes from the anchored self-proofs. Secrecy is explicitly not claimed. No fsync is performed anywhere, so no directory-fsync semantics are claimed on any platform.

Every host call (whoami, both icacls invocations, chmod, stat) is wrapped; no exception escapes protect(). Both external tools run with a 10s timeout and windowsHide, so a hung host tool refuses instead of stalling a restore. Apply-side faults map to UNAVAILABLE and read-back-side faults to UNVERIFIABLE — two distinct codes for two distinct facts.
